opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons, and they're quite interesting because they tell you something about the nature of these domains.

The first is that coding and mathematics are, in a sense, closed systems with very clear rules. You can verify whether an answer is right. A program either compiles and passes its tests or it doesn't. A proof either checks out or it doesn't. That verifiability is incredibly powerful, because it means you can generate enormous amounts of synthetic data and use reinforcement learning effectively. You have a reliable reward signal, which is exactly what we exploited with AlphaGo and AlphaZero in games. Games, maths, and code all share that property: there's an objective way to score how well you're doing.

The second reason is that there's a huge amount of high-quality data available, especially for code. Decades of open-source software, documentation, discussions about bugs and fixes. And mathematics has this beautifully structured body of knowledge built up over centuries, where each result rests on the ones before it.

The third reason, which I find most fascinating, is that we tend to think of maths and coding as the pinnacle of human intellectual difficulty, because they're hard for *us*. But that's a bit of an illusion. Evolution didn't optimize our brains for symbolic manipulation; it optimized them for navigating messy physical and social environments. So things we find effortless, like picking up a cup, understanding a subtle social cue, or common-sense reasoning about the physical world, are actually much harder to capture. That's a version of Moravec's paradox, I suppose.

What's still genuinely hard, even within maths, is the creative part: not solving a well-posed conjecture, but coming up with the conjecture worth solving in the first place, or inventing a new field the way someone like Riemann or Galois did. That's a different level of capability, and I don't think we're there yet. Asking the right question is often much harder than answering it, and I suspect that's one of the remaining hallmarks we'll need to crack on the path to AGI.

r001.rationale: The response says coding and mathematics have proved relatively easy for AI, despite people viewing them as difficult intellectual skills.

r002.rationale: It links verifiable answers to generating enormous amounts of synthetic data and using reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to a few things. The first is verification. In coding and in mathematics, you have a very clear signal about whether you've got the right answer. Does the code compile, does it pass the tests, does the proof check out. That's enormously important for a learning system, because you can generate lots of attempts, check them, and then train on the ones that work. It's not that different in spirit from what we did with AlphaGo and AlphaZero, where the rules of the game give you a perfect simulator and a clean reward. Maths and code are, in a sense, the closest thing we have in the real world to that kind of closed, well-defined domain.

The second thing is data. There's a huge amount of high-quality code and mathematical reasoning written down, and crucially a lot of it includes the working, the intermediate steps, not just the final answer. So the systems can learn the process, not just the outputs.

And the third, which I find quite interesting philosophically, is that these are domains where the abstractions are already very clean. Humans have spent centuries compressing mathematics into a formal language that strips out ambiguity. Code is the same, it's designed to be unambiguous. So the model doesn't have to deal with all the messiness of the physical world, or of human intentions, or of common sense, which is where I think things get much harder. If you contrast that with, say, robotics, or genuinely novel scientific discovery, where you have to form hypotheses about a world you can't fully simulate and the feedback is noisy and slow, you can see why progress there has been more uneven.

I'd add one caveat, though. Being good at competition maths or at writing working code is not quite the same as being a great mathematician or a great engineer. The really hard part is knowing which problem is worth solving, coming up with the conjecture in the first place, having taste. I think we're starting to see glimmers of that, but it's still, in my view, the frontier.

r001.rationale: The response directly explains why coding and mathematics have been relatively easy for AI systems to learn, contrasting their clean, well-defined feedback with harder domains.

r002.rationale: It describes generating many coding or math attempts, verifying them, and training on the successful ones, which conveys verified synthetic training data.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key is that you can check the answers. I wouldn’t say coding and mathematics are easy in an absolute sense, but they have this very useful property: you can get quite precise feedback on whether you’re making progress.

With code, you can run it. Does it compile? Does it pass the tests? With mathematics, at least when you’ve formalized the problem, you can check whether a proof is valid. So the system can attempt a solution, get feedback, and improve. That gives you a very powerful learning loop, somewhat analogous to games, where you have clear rules and a clear outcome.

And there’s a lot of structure in these domains. They’re built out of rules and abstractions that you can combine. There’s also a substantial amount of written material for systems to learn from.

Compare that with something like judging whether a scientific hypothesis is useful. You might need to do an experiment in the real world, and that could take months. Or judging whether a piece of writing is truly great—there isn’t a simple test you can run. So I think it’s less that mathematics and coding are inherently easy, and more that they provide unusually good conditions for learning.

r001.rationale: The response explains why coding and mathematics offer unusually favorable learning conditions for AI, communicating their relative ease despite not being easy in an absolute sense.

r002.rationale: It cites precise feedback and verifiable code or proofs, but does not attribute the advantage to synthetic training data.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’m not sure I’d call them easy, but they have a property that makes them particularly suited to learning: you can check the answers. With mathematics, you can often verify a proof, and with code, you can run it and see whether it passes the tests. So you have this very powerful feedback loop where the system can attempt a solution, get feedback, and improve.

They’re also quite self-contained. The rules are explicit, and a lot of the information you need is there in the problem statement. Compare that with operating in the real world, where you’re dealing with uncertainty, missing information, and sometimes even disagreement about what a good outcome looks like.

Of course, producing a genuinely new mathematical insight or building a large, reliable software system is still very difficult. But having an objective way to assess progress gives you a tremendous advantage.

r001.rationale: The response says coding and mathematics are suited to learning, but it does not communicate that traditionally difficult skills have counterintuitively proved relatively easy for AI; it even qualifies that it would not call them easy.

r002.rationale: It cites checkable answers and feedback from proofs or tests, but does not attribute this to the availability of synthetic training data.
